questions.question: How do you read a Java stack trace to find the source of an error?
questions.title: How to Read a Java Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: A Java stack trace reads **top to bottom from most recent call to oldest**. The **first line** is the exception type and message; the **`at` lines** below are the call stack, with the topmost `at` being where the exception was actually thrown. To debug, find the **first `at` line that's in *your* code** — that's almost always where to start.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can systematically read a stack trace to locate the failure, not just panic at the wall of text.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading bottom-up looking for the cause, or jumping to framework lines instead of finding your own code in the trace.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the exception line vs the at lines, the top of stack = throw point, and scanning for the first line in your own package.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **First line** = exception type + message (what went wrong).
- **`at` lines** = call stack, **most recent first**; top = throw point.
- Scan for the **first `at` line in your own package** to start debugging.
- Each `at` line gives **Class.method(File.java:line)** — go straight there.
- Check for **`Caused by:`** for the underlying origin.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A Java stack trace looks intimidating, but it has a very predictable structure, and you read it from the top down. The very first line tells you what went wrong — the exception type, like NullPointerException, and a message that often tells you exactly what was null or out of bounds. Below that come the at lines, and those are the call stack. The crucial thing to know is the order: they're listed most recent first. So the topmost at line is the exact place the exception was thrown, and each line below it is the method that called the one above, all the way down to main or the entry point at the bottom. So my reading process is: first line tells me what, top at line tells me where it was thrown. But here's the practical trick — the top line is often inside a library, like Spring or the JDK, which isn't where my bug is. So I scan down the at lines until I find the first one that's in my own package, my own code. That line, with its file name and line number in the format Class dot method, file colon line, is almost always where I should start debugging. I open that file at that line and look at what could be null or wrong there. The last thing I check is whether there's a Caused by section further down, because that points to the underlying exception that triggered everything — and that's frequently the real origin of the problem. The mistakes people make are reading bottom-up looking for the cause, or getting lost in framework lines instead of finding their own code.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g.

`com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

Reading bottom-up looking for the cause, or jumping to framework lines instead of finding your own code in the trace.

sections.title: Reading Order
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Line 1: Exception type + message
WHAT went wrong] --> B[Top 'at' line
WHERE it was thrown] B --> C[Scan down for first
line in YOUR package] C --> D[Open that file:line
start debugging here] D --> E{Caused by: present?} E -->|Yes| F[Read the cause
for the real origin] ```

sections.title: Anatomy of a Trace
sections.content:
```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke
    "String.length()" because "name" is null          <-- (1) WHAT
    at com.app.UserService.greet(UserService.java:25)   <-- (2) WHERE it was thrown (your code)
    at com.app.UserController.hello(UserController.java:14) <-- (3) caller (your code)
    at org.springframework.web...invoke(...)            <-- (4) framework, ignore for now
```

Read it as: a NullPointerException (1) was thrown at `UserService.java:25` (2), which was called from `UserController.java:14` (3). Start at line 25.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading bottom-up**: the bottom is `main`/the entry point, not the failure; the top `at` is the throw point.
- **Stopping at framework lines**: the top line is often library code — scan down to *your* package.
- **Ignoring the message**: the first line often says exactly what was null or out of range.

questions.question: What does 'Caused by' in a Java stack trace mean and how do you use it?
questions.title: Caused By — Nested Exceptions in Java Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: **`Caused by:`** marks a **chained (wrapped) exception** — a lower-level exception that triggered the one above it. Java prints the outer exception first, then `Caused by:` for each underlying cause, deepest last. The **root cause is usually the *last* `Caused by:` block**, so that's where you look for the real origin of the failure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know that 'Caused by' shows exception chaining and that the root cause is the deepest one.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Debugging only the top exception (e.g. a generic wrapper) instead of following the chain to the real root cause.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain wrapping with new RuntimeException(msg, cause) preserves the chain, and that the last Caused by is the origin.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Caused by:`** = a wrapped (chained) underlying exception.
- Outer exception prints first; **deepest/last `Caused by:` is the root cause**.
- Preserve the chain with **`new XException(msg, cause)`**.
- The top exception adds *context*; the bottom cause is the *origin*.
- Dropping the cause throws away your best debugging clue.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Caused by in a stack trace marks a chained, or wrapped, exception. It happens because of a really common pattern: a lower layer throws a technical exception, like a SQLException, and a higher layer catches it and rethrows something more meaningful for its own level, like a ServiceException, but it passes the original exception along as the cause. When Java prints that, you get the outer exception at the top, and then one or more Caused by sections below it, each one the underlying exception that triggered the one above. The key insight for debugging is that the root cause — the thing you actually need to fix — is the deepest one, the last Caused by in the chain. The exceptions above it are wrappers that add context about which layer the problem bubbled up through. So if I see ServiceException checkout failed at the top, caused by a DataAccessException, caused by a SQLException connection refused at the very bottom, the real problem is the database connection, not the ServiceException. I go straight to that last Caused by. The big mistake people make is debugging only the top exception, which is often a vague wrapper, and missing the specific root cause down at the bottom. The other side of this, as a developer, is making sure you preserve the chain when you rethrow. If you catch an exception and throw a new one, you must pass the original as the cause — new ServiceException of the message comma e. If you leave off that cause, the trace shows your wrapper with no Caused by at all, and you've thrown away the single most useful piece of debugging information.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g.

`com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

**`Caused by:`** marks a **chained (wrapped) exception** — a lower-level exception that triggered the one above it. Java prints the outer exception first, then `Caused by:` for each underlying cause, deepest last. The **root cause is usually the *last* `Caused by:` block**, so that's where you look for the real origin of the failure.

sections.title: Following the Chain
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Top exception
ServiceException: checkout failed] --> B[Caused by:
DataAccessException] B --> C[Caused by:
SQLException: connection refused] C --> D[Root cause = last 'Caused by'
fix the DB connection here] ```

sections.title: Swallowing the Cause — Chain Lost
Wrapping with the Cause — Chain Preserved
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Debugging only the top exception**: the wrapper is generic; the last `Caused by:` is the real problem.
- **Dropping the cause when rethrowing**: `new Wrapper(msg)` without `, e` deletes the chain.
- **Confusing order**: the root cause is the *deepest* / last `Caused by:`, not the first line.

questions.question: How do you read a NullPointerException stack trace in Java?
questions.title: Reading a NullPointerException Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: A NullPointerException stack trace's **first line names the exception**, and since Java 14+ the **helpful NPE message says exactly which variable was null** (e.g. `Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "name" is null`). The **top `at` line** is the file and line where you dereferenced null — go there, and trace back to *why* that reference was never assigned.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can pinpoint the exact null dereference from the trace, including using the modern helpful NPE message.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Knowing it's an NPE but not reading the message/line to identify which reference was null and why.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention helpful NullPointerExceptions (JEP 358, Java 14+) naming the variable, and tracing back to the assignment that returned null.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- NPE = calling a method/field on a **null reference**.
- **Java 14+ helpful NPE** names the exact null variable in the message.
- Top **`at` line** = file:line of the dereference — go there first.
- Trace **backwards** to why the variable was null (map miss, uninit field, null return).
- Fix the **source**, not just the crash site.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Reading a NullPointerException trace is one of the most common debugging tasks, and modern Java makes it much easier than it used to be. The first line says java.lang.NullPointerException, and since Java 14, with the helpful NullPointerExceptions feature, the message tells you exactly which reference was null. Instead of just NullPointerException, you get something like cannot invoke String.length because name is null. That single message often tells you almost everything — which variable, and what you tried to do to it. Then the top at line gives you the file and line number of the actual dereference, so I go straight there. But finding the line where it crashed is only half the job. The real question is why that variable was null in the first place, so I trace backwards. I look at what assigned that variable. Maybe it came from a map's get method that returned null because the key wasn't present. Maybe it's a field that was never initialized. Maybe it's the return value of a method that can return null. That upstream source is where the actual fix belongs. For example, if I called users.get(id) and that returned null because the id wasn't in the map, the fix isn't just to slap a null check at the crash site — it's to decide what should happen when the user is genuinely absent, whether that's returning a default, throwing a clearer exception, or using Optional to express that the value might not be there. So the workflow is: read the helpful message to see which variable, jump to the top at line to see where, then trace back to understand why it was null and fix it at the source.

sections.content:
In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g.

`com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

The **top `at` line** is the file and line where you dereferenced null — go there, and trace back to *why* that reference was never assigned.

sections.title: From NPE to Root
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[NPE first line
which var is null] --> B[Top 'at' line
file:line of dereference] B --> C[What assigned that variable?] C --> D{Source of null} D --> E[Map/get returned null] D --> F[Field never initialized] D --> G[Method returned null] ```

sections.title: The Bug — Unguarded Null
The Fix — Guard or Optional
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Ignoring the helpful message**: on Java 14+ it literally names the null variable — read it.
- **Fixing the symptom**: adding a null check at the crash site without asking why it was null upstream.
- **Confusing reference vs object**: the *variable* is null, not the method you called on it.

questions.question: How do you identify your own code versus framework code in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Identifying Your Code vs Framework Code in a Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g. `com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can quickly separate your code from framework noise in a long trace to find the actionable frame.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting lost in or blaming framework/JDK frames instead of locating your own package's frame.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention recognizing package prefixes, IDE features that fold library frames, and that the framework usually just called your handler.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Your frames** start with your project package; **framework frames** start with `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.*`.
- The bug is almost always in **your** code — find the topmost frame in your package.
- Framework frames above your code are just the **plumbing that called you**.
- IDEs can **fold/collapse library frames** to reduce noise.
- Don't blame mature libraries before checking your own adjacent frame.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The trick to reading a long stack trace is quickly separating your code from framework code, and you do that by recognizing package prefixes. Your own code's frames start with your project's package — something like com.myapp. Framework and JDK frames start with prefixes like java dot, jakarta dot, org dot springframework, org dot hibernate, or org dot apache. A real trace in a Spring app might be forty lines long, but maybe only two or three of those are actually your code; the rest is the framework's plumbing calling into your handler and back out. Since bugs live in your own code far more often than in mature, heavily-tested libraries, my approach is to scan down past all the framework noise and find the topmost at line that's in my own package. That line is nearest to the actual failure within my code, and it's where I start debugging — I open that file at that line number. The framework frames above it are usually just Spring dispatching the request to my controller, so they're not where the problem is. Most IDEs even help here — IntelliJ can fold or collapse library frames so you only see your own code in the trace. The mistake I see freshers make is either reading every single frame and getting overwhelmed, or assuming the framework is broken because its name appears at the top of the trace, when really the bug is in the com.myapp line sitting right underneath. So: recognize the prefixes, ignore the plumbing, and zero in on the topmost frame that belongs to you.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g.

`com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

Long traces are mostly **framework plumbing**. The fast way to cut through it: recognize **package prefixes**. Frames in *your* code start with your project package (`com.myapp.*`); framework/JDK frames start with `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.springframework.`, `org.hibernate.`, `org.apache.`, etc. Bugs live in your code far more often than in mature libraries, so find the **topmost `at` line in your own package** — that's your entry point into debugging.

Reading bottom-up looking for the cause, or jumping to framework lines instead of finding your own code in the trace.

sections.title: Telling Frames Apart
sections.content:
emerald|Your code|~Start debugging here|com.myapp.*|your package prefix|topmost = focus
blue|Framework|~Just plumbing|org.springframework.*|org.hibernate.*|usually not the bug
amber|JDK|~Standard library|java.* / jakarta.*|rarely your bug|skip past
rose|Tip|~IDE folds these|collapse library frames|jump to your line|less noise

sections.title: Spotting Your Frame
sections.content:
```text
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: id must be positive
    at java.base/java.util.Objects.checkIndex(...)         <- JDK (skip)
    at org.springframework.web...invokeHandlerMethod(...)  <- framework (skip)
    at com.myapp.order.OrderService.find(OrderService.java:31)  <- YOUR code: START HERE
    at com.myapp.order.OrderController.get(OrderController.java:18) <- your caller
    at org.springframework.web...doDispatch(...)           <- framework (skip)
```

The two `com.myapp` lines are yours; everything else is the framework calling into (and out of) your handler.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Blaming the library**: assuming Spring/Hibernate is broken when the bug is in the `com.myapp` frame just below.
- **Reading every frame**: wading through dozens of framework lines instead of scanning for your package.
- **Missing your deepest frame**: focus on the **topmost** of your own frames — that's nearest the failure.

questions.question: What does a StackOverflowError stack trace look like and what causes it?
questions.title: StackOverflowError — What It Looks Like and Why It Happens
questions.direct_answer: A **StackOverflowError** trace shows the **same method(s) repeated over and over** — the signature of **unbounded recursion**. It occurs when recursive calls never reach a base case, so stack frames pile up until the fixed-size call stack is exhausted. It's a `java.lang.Error` (not an `Exception`); fix it by adding a reachable base case or converting to iteration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize the repeating-frames signature and know the root cause is recursion without a reachable base case.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing it with OutOfMemoryError, or not realizing the repeating frames pinpoint the runaway recursion.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note it's an Error not an Exception, mention mutual/accidental recursion, and that iteration avoids the stack.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- StackOverflowError = **call stack exhausted**, an `Error`, not an `Exception`.
- Cause is almost always **unbounded recursion** (missing/unreachable base case).
- The trace shows the **same methods repeating** — that names the culprit.
- Fix: add a **reachable base case** or rewrite as **iteration**.
- Watch for **mutual recursion** and accidental self-calls in getters/`toString()`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A StackOverflowError means the call stack has run out of space, and in practice the cause is almost always recursion that never stops. Every time a method is called, the JVM pushes a new frame onto the thread's stack to hold its local variables and return address. The stack is a fixed size, so if a method keeps calling itself without ever hitting a base case that lets it return, the frames pile up until the stack is full, and then the JVM throws StackOverflowError. One thing worth noting is that it's an Error, not an Exception — it signals a serious condition you're not really meant to catch and recover from; you're meant to fix the code. The stack trace for this is actually very easy to recognize, because you'll see the same one or two methods repeated over and over, hundreds or thousands of times. That repetition immediately tells you which recursion is the problem. The classic example is a recursive factorial or fibonacci where the base case is missing or wrong — like a factorial that always calls factorial of n minus one but never checks for n less than or equal to one, so it recurses past zero forever. The fix is to make sure there's a base case that's actually reachable, or, for inputs that could recurse very deeply, to rewrite the logic as an iterative loop, which doesn't add stack frames at all. Two subtler causes to watch for are mutual recursion, where method a calls b and b calls a with no termination, and accidental recursion, like a getter that calls itself or a toString that references itself. But the diagnosis is always the same: look at the repeating method in the trace, and that's your unbounded recursion.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g.

`com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

A **StackOverflowError** trace shows the **same method(s) repeated over and over** — the signature of **unbounded recursion**. It occurs when recursive calls never reach a base case, so stack frames pile up until the fixed-size call stack is exhausted. It's a `java.lang.Error` (not an `Exception`); fix it by adding a reachable base case or converting to iteration.

Reading bottom-up looking for the cause, or jumping to framework lines instead of finding your own code in the trace.

sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[method calls itself] --> B{base case reached?} B -->|No / never| C[push another stack frame] C --> A B -->|Yes| D[returns - stack unwinds] C --> E[stack space exhausted
StackOverflowError] ```

sections.title: The Bug — Missing/Wrong Base Case
The Fix — Reachable Base Case (or Iterate)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No base case** (or one that's unreachable, e.g. `n != 0` with a step that skips 0).
- **Mutual recursion**: `a()` calls `b()` which calls `a()` with no termination.
- **Accidental recursion**: a getter calling itself, or `toString()`/`equals()` referencing themselves.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with SLF4J and Logback logging
speakable_v2.hook: A StackOverflowError trace is the easiest one to diagnose — the same method screaming back at you a thousand times is pointing right at the bug.

beats.heading: What you see
beats.body: Every method call adds a frame to the call stack. When a method calls itself recursively without a base case to stop it, frames pile up until the JVM's stack memory runs out. The stack trace shows the same method name repeated hundreds of times — that repetition is your immediate clue.

beats.heading: How to fix it
items: Identify the repeating method name in the stack trace.
Open that method and look for the base case — is it missing or unreachable?
Add or correct the base case.
For very deep legitimate recursion, consider converting to an iterative approach with an explicit stack.

beats.heading: candidates miss
beats.body: StackOverflowError is an Error, not an Exception. Don't catch and suppress it — that hides a broken algorithm. The right fix is always to repair the recursion logic itself.

speakable_v2.cap: Repeated method names in the trace means infinite recursion. Find the missing base case and fix it — never catch and suppress a StackOverflowError.

questions.question: What is a chained exception (exception cause) in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Chained Exceptions in Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: A **chained exception** is an exception that holds another as its **cause** — created with `new XException(msg, cause)`. In the stack trace it shows as **`Caused by:`** blocks, and the **deepest/last one is the root cause**. Chaining lets a higher layer throw a meaningful exception while preserving the original low-level error for debugging.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand exception chaining via cause and that the deepest Caused by is the real origin.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Rethrowing without passing the cause, destroying the chain and the root-cause information.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the layering motivation (meaningful exceptions per layer) and preserving the cause when wrapping.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A chained exception holds another as its **cause**.
- Created via **`new XException(msg, cause)`** (or `initCause`).
- Trace prints **`Caused by:`** per link; **deepest = root cause**.
- Preserve the cause when rethrowing — it's your key diagnostic.
- Wrap low-level checked exceptions in meaningful higher-level ones, with the cause.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A chained exception is an exception that carries another exception inside it as its cause, and you see it in a stack trace as the Caused by sections. It comes from a very normal layering pattern. A low-level component throws something technical, like a SQLException. A higher layer doesn't want to expose that database detail to its callers, so it catches the SQLException and throws a more meaningful exception for its own level, like a ServiceException — but, crucially, it passes the original SQLException along as the cause, using the constructor that takes a message and a cause. When that gets printed, you see the ServiceException first, then Caused by, then the SQLException underneath. You can have several links in the chain. The rule for debugging is that the root cause — the thing you actually fix — is the deepest one, the last Caused by at the bottom. The exceptions above it are wrappers that tell you which layer the problem passed through. As a developer, the key responsibility is to always preserve the cause when you rethrow. If you create a new exception but forget to pass the original as the cause, the trace shows your wrapper with no Caused by at all, and you've discarded the most useful debugging information you had. Chaining is also how you cleanly convert a checked exception into an unchecked one without polluting every method signature, while still keeping the full diagnostic trail. So: chained exceptions wrap a cause, the deepest Caused by is the origin, and you must always pass the cause along.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g.

`com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

A **chained exception** is an exception that holds another as its **cause** — created with `new XException(msg, cause)`. In the stack trace it shows as **`Caused by:`** blocks, and the **deepest/last one is the root cause**. Chaining lets a higher layer throw a meaningful exception while preserving the original low-level error for debugging.

Reading bottom-up looking for the cause, or jumping to framework lines instead of finding your own code in the trace.

sections.title: The Cause Chain
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[ServiceException
checkout failed] -->|Caused by| B[DataAccessException] B -->|Caused by| C[SQLException
connection refused] C --> D[Root cause = deepest link
fix here] ```

sections.title: Losing the Cause
Preserving the Cause
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Dropping the cause** when rethrowing (`new Wrapper(msg)` without `, e`).
- **Debugging the wrapper** instead of the deepest `Caused by:`.
- **Over-wrapping**: re-wrapping the same exception at every layer adds noise without context.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with SLF4J and Logback logging
speakable_v2.hook: Exception chaining is how a clean ServiceException at the top still remembers the messy SQLException that actually broke at the bottom.

beats.heading: Why chaining exists
beats.body: Each layer of your application catches a low-level exception and re-throws it wrapped in a higher-level one. A SQLException becomes a DataAccessException becomes a ServiceException. Each layer adds context, but the original problem is preserved in the chain.

beats.heading: Reading the chain correctly
items: The top exception is the outermost wrapper — it tells you which layer failed.
Each 'Caused by:' is one level deeper toward the origin.
Always scroll to the last 'Caused by:' — that's the actual root cause.
The fix typically lives near that last entry, not near the top.

beats.heading: non-obvious
beats.body: You create a chained exception by passing the original to the constructor: throw new ServiceException('message', originalException). If you only pass the message string, you silently discard the original cause — and that makes debugging much harder.

speakable_v2.cap: Bottom of the Caused-by chain first, always. That's the root cause. Work upward only if you need to understand which layer introduced the wrapping.

questions.question: What does 'at' mean in a Java stack trace and how do you use it to find the bug?
questions.title: Reading the 'at' Lines in Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: Each **`at` line** is one **stack frame** — a method that was executing — in the format `at package.Class.method(File.java:line)`. They're listed **most recent first**, so the **top `at` line is where the exception was thrown**. To find the bug, read the top `at` line, then scan down to the first `at` line in **your own package** and open that exact `File.java:line`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can decode an 'at' line into class/method/file/line and use ordering to locate the failure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing 'at' lines are ordered newest-first, or ignoring the file:line that points straight to the code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain each at line is a call frame, top = throw point, and the File.java:line is a direct jump target in the IDE.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Each **`at` line = a stack frame** (a method that was executing).
- Format: **`at package.Class.method(File.java:line)`**.
- Ordered **most recent first**; **top `at` = throw point**.
- **File.java:line** jumps you straight to the code in the IDE.
- Find the first `at` line in **your package** to start debugging.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The at lines in a stack trace are the heart of it — each one represents a single stack frame, which is a method that was in the middle of executing when the exception was thrown. The format is at, then the fully-qualified class name, a dot, the method name, and then in parentheses the source file and the line number, like at com.app.Calc.divide, Calc.java colon 12. The most important thing to understand is the ordering: the at lines are listed most recent first. So the very top at line is the exact place the exception was thrown, and each line below it is the method that called the one above, working down to main or the entry point at the very bottom. To use this to find a bug, I read the top at line to see where it was thrown, and I pay close attention to that File dot java colon line part, because that's a precise pointer — in IntelliJ or Eclipse it's actually clickable, and it'll take me straight to that line in the source. If the top at line is in a framework or the JDK, I scan down to the first at line that's in my own package, because that's where my code is involved. So with an example like an ArithmeticException, divide by zero, the top at line says Calc.java line 12, the next says it was called from run at line 6, and the bottom says main at line 4 — that tells me the whole call path, and I start at Calc.java line 12. The mistake people make is reading from the bottom, where main is, instead of the top where the actual throw happened.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g.

`com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

Each **`at` line** is one **stack frame** — a method that was executing — in the format `at package.Class.method(File.java:line)`. They're listed **most recent first**, so the **top `at` line is where the exception was thrown**. To find the bug, read the top `at` line, then scan down to the first `at` line in **your own package** and open that exact `File.java:line`.

Reading bottom-up looking for the cause, or jumping to framework lines instead of finding your own code in the trace.

sections.title: Anatomy of an 'at' Line
sections.content:
blue|package.Class|~Where|com.app.OrderService|which class|your code vs framework
emerald|.method|~What ran|the method executing|in that frame|the call
amber|(File.java:line)|~Exact spot|clickable in IDE|go here|the line number
rose|Order|~Newest first|top = throw point|down = callers|bottom = main

sections.title: Decoding 'at' Lines
sections.content:
```text
java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
    at com.app.Calc.divide(Calc.java:12)   <- thrown HERE (top, your code)
    at com.app.Calc.run(Calc.java:6)        <- called divide()
    at com.app.Main.main(Main.java:4)       <- program entry (bottom)
```

Reads as: `divide` (Calc.java line 12) threw the exception; it was called by `run` (line 6), which was called by `main` (line 4). Open `Calc.java:12` first.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading bottom-up**: the bottom is `main`, not the failure; the top `at` is the throw point.
- **Ignoring File.java:line**: it's a direct jump target — use it.
- **Skipping your own frames**: scan past framework `at` lines to the first one in your package.

speakable_v2.hook: Every 'at' line is a clickable breadcrumb — the top one drops you exactly where the exception was thrown, file and line included.

beats.heading: What each line contains
beats.body: The format is: at FullyQualifiedClassName.methodName(FileName.java:lineNumber). The topmost 'at' line is where the exception was actually thrown. Every line below it is the method that called the one above — reading downward shows you how execution got to the throw site.

beats.heading: Practical strategy
items: Read the exception type and message first.
Find the topmost 'at' line that matches your application package.
Open that file at that exact line number.

beats.heading: gotcha
